files.codex/u1-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students solve adding-to, taking-from and putting-together story problems within 20 using drawings, objects and number sentences (1.OA.A.1).
- Students relate counting to addition and subtraction by counting on and counting back (1.OA.C.5).
- Students add and subtract within 20 using counting on and other strategies, building fluency within 10 (1.OA.C.6).

MATERIALS
- Counters (or small snacks, buttons or bottle caps from the class counting collections)
- A number path or number line from 0 to 20 for each student
- Ten frames (two per student, to show numbers to 20)
- Whiteboards and markers, or tablets with the class activities open for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Story Problems together. Act out a story with students as birds: 12 birds on a tree (12 students stand), 4 fly away (4 sit). How many are left? Write 12 - 4 = 8 together.
Day 2: Lesson activity: Count On, Count Back. Model on the number path: start at 8, hop 3 to 11. Students try each question with the number path, then tell a partner why we start with the bigger number.
Day 3: Apple Orchard Story Problems. Read each story aloud twice. Students solve with counters or drawings and write a number sentence; photograph or draw their work.
Day 4: Make Your Own Story Problem. Model one about the class pet or lunch. Students draw and record their own story, then trade with a partner to solve.
Day 5: Assessment: Adding and Taking Away Check. Read each problem aloud. Students work alone with counters and number paths available. Note who counts all and who counts on.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep numbers within 10 at first (6 apples and 3 more), and let students act out the story with counters before drawing it.
- Support: give a number sentence frame with boxes (__ + __ = __) to fill in.
- Stretch: offer change-unknown stories (Bear had 8 apples. She picked some more. Now she has 13. How many did she pick?) and ask for two different ways to solve one problem.
- Multilingual learners: pre-teach story words with pictures and gestures: more, left, in all, fly away, picks. Act each one out. Let students tell their own story problem in their home language first.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
This month we are solving story problems by drawing pictures, using counters, and counting on. You can make up story problems at home: "You have 7 grapes. I give you 4 more. How many now?" Ask your child to show you how they figured it out. Counting on from the bigger number (7... 8, 9, 10, 11) is a great strategy to praise.",
  "id": "u1-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Adding and Taking Away Within 20",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

files.codex/u2-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students understand that the two digits of a two-digit number stand for tens and ones (1.NBT.B.2).
- Students understand 10 as a bundle of ten ones, the numbers 11 to 19 as a ten and some ones (1.NBT.B.2b), and 10, 20, 30 ... 90 as some tens and 0 ones (1.NBT.B.2c).

MATERIALS
- Straws or craft sticks and rubber bands, for bundling tens
- The class counting collections (buttons, pasta, bottle caps) in bags of 20 to 60
- Base-ten rods and cubes, or connecting cubes snapped in trains of ten
- A tens and ones mat (two columns) for each student
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Bundles of Ten together. Each pair counts a counting collection by making groups of ten in cups. Record: how many tens? how many ones left? how many in all?
Day 2: Lesson activity: Sam's Straws. Read the story aloud, then rebuild it with real straws and rubber bands. Students answer, then tell a partner why counting by tens is faster.
Day 3: Tens and Ones. Students build each number on a tens and ones mat, then show their work. Spend time on 50 (5 tens and 0 ones) and the teen number 17.
Day 4: Draw It With Tens. Model quick drawings: a stick for each ten, a dot for each one. Students draw 26 and 41 and record themselves telling the tens and ones.
Day 5: Assessment: Tens and Ones Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use cubes and their mats. Watch for students who reverse the digits (writing 74 for 7 ones and 4 tens).

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep to numbers under 50 and always build with real objects before drawing. Use a mat with a picture of a ten-stick at the top of the tens column.
- Support: for teen numbers, start with a full ten frame plus some loose counters.
- Stretch: ask for a number shown two ways (34 is 3 tens and 4 ones, or 2 tens and 14 ones) and numbers to 120 (11 tens is 110).
- Multilingual learners: say "tens" and "ones" while touching the bundle and the single straw every time. Note that teen number names in English hide the ten (eleven, twelve) and say the ones first (fourteen); many languages say "ten-four". Invite students to count in their home language and compare.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning that big numbers are made of tens and ones: 34 is 3 tens and 4 ones. Please send in a small bag of buttons, pasta or bottle caps for our counting collections if you can. At home, count a pile of something together by making groups of ten. Ask your child: how many tens? How many left over? How many in all?",
  "id": "u2-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Tens and Ones",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

The tens digit goes up by 1 each time (10 more); the ones digit stays 3.\nNumbers to 120 Check: 1. 109, 110, 111. 2. 112. 3. 47 < 74. 4. 66. 5. 90. 6. 48 (the number is 38).\nScoring tip: a correct comparison written in words (\"34 is less than 43\") is Got it! on comparing if the student cannot yet form the symbol; teach the symbol next. For 10 more and 10 less, a student who counts by ones to get the right answer is Getting there: the goal is to change the tens digit without counting.",

files.codex/u3-overview.json:
{
  "body": "We can count past 100! 💯\n... 98, 99, 100, 101, 102 ... all the way to 120.\nTens help us compare: 52 is more than 25, because 5 tens is more than 2 tens.\nTens help us jump: 10 more than 34 is 44.\nIn this unit we will count far, compare numbers and jump by tens.",
  "id": "u3-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Counting Up to 120",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u3-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students count to 120 starting at any number, and read and write numerals in that range (1.NBT.A.1).
- Students compare two two-digit numbers using the meaning of the tens and ones digits, recording comparisons with >, = and < (1.NBT.B.3).
- Students mentally find 10 more and 10 less than a two-digit number and explain their reasoning (1.NBT.C.5).
- Students add a two-digit and a one-digit number, add multiples of ten, and subtract multiples of ten (1.NBT.C.4, 1.NBT.C.6).

MATERIALS
- A 120 chart for each student and a large class 120 chart
- Base-ten rods and cubes, or ten-trains of connecting cubes
- Greater-than and less-than cards (an open mouth or arrow that points to the smaller number)
- Number cards 0 to 9 for building and comparing two-digit numbers
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Counting Up to 120 together. Count around the circle from 95 to 120. Find 100 on the class chart and look at the rows below it: what pattern do you see? Lesson activity: Counting Past 100.
Day 2: Compare with base-ten blocks: build 34 and 43 side by side. Which has more tens? Introduce >, < and = (the symbol opens toward the bigger number). Students start Greater Than, Less Than.
Day 3: Finish Greater Than, Less Than. Play Compare: each partner draws two digit cards, makes the biggest number they can, and records the comparison.
Day 4: Jump by Tens. On the 120 chart, move down a row for 10 more and up a row for 10 less. Add tens with rods (4 tens and 3 tens is 7 tens). Students complete Jump by Tens.
Day 5: Assessment: Numbers to 120 Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use their 120 charts for problems 1 and 2 only.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep comparisons to numbers with different tens digits first (34 and 52) before the same tens digit (34 and 38). Use base-ten blocks for every comparison.
- Support: for 10 more and 10 less, add or remove one rod and say what changed. Use the 120 chart rows.
- Stretch: compare three numbers and put them in order; find 20 more and 20 less; write the numbers from 120 down to 100.
- Multilingual learners: teach "greater than", "less than", "equal to", "more" and "less" with blocks and gestures. Number words past 100 can be tricky in English (one hundred one, not one hundred and one in math class); practice saying them with the chart.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are counting all the way to 120, comparing numbers and jumping by tens. At home, try counting together from a number other than 1, such as 87 or 105. Compare prices or page numbers: which is bigger, 46 or 64? How do you know? Ask your child what number is 10 more than their age, or 10 more than the number of steps to your door.",
  "id": "u3-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Numbers to 120",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

True; both sides are 10. 6. 14 (3 + 7 = 10, 10 + 4 = 14). 7. 7 children.\nScoring tip: on \"I can use a strategy\", count the strategy the student shows, not only the answer: a right answer reached by counting all from 1 is Getting there. files.codex/u4-overview.json:
{
  "body": "There are many smart ways to add and subtract. 🧠\nMake a ten: 9 + 4 is 9 + 1 + 3, so it is 10 + 3 = 13.\nUse doubles: 6 + 6 = 12, so 6 + 7 = 13.\nThink addition to subtract: 13 - 5 is the number that makes 5 + __ = 13.\nThe equal sign means \"is the same as\".\nIn this unit we will try each way and pick our favorites.",
  "id": "u4-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Smart Ways to Add and Subtract",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u4-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students add and subtract within 20 using making ten, doubles and near doubles, and the relationship between addition and subtraction (1.OA.C.6).
- Students apply properties of operations as strategies: changing the order of addends, and grouping three addends to make a ten (1.OA.B.3).
- Students understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem (1.OA.B.4) and find the unknown number in an equation (1.OA.D.8).
- Students understand the equal sign and decide whether equations are true or false (1.OA.D.7).
- Students solve word problems with three addends (1.OA.A.2) and with a start or change unknown (1.OA.A.1).

MATERIALS
- Two ten frames per student and two colors of counters
- Number bond mats (a whole and two parts)
- A balance scale or a drawn balance, for showing that both sides of the equal sign are the same
- Fact family triangle cards
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Smart Ways to Add and Subtract together. Lesson activity: Make a Ten. Model 9 + 4 on two ten frames: slide one counter to fill the first frame. Students solve the questions with counters and explain one to a partner.
Day 2: Doubles and near doubles: build 6 + 6 and 6 + 7 with cubes. Then number bonds: show 4 and 7 make 11, and write all four facts. Students start Fact Families and Missing Numbers.
Day 3: Finish Fact Families and Missing Numbers. Talk through the shell story: what do we know, and what is missing? Show it as ? + 5 = 13.
Day 4: The equal sign means "is the same as". Use the balance: is 4 + 1 the same as 5 + 2? Students complete True or False?, looking for a ten in three-number problems.
Day 5: Assessment: Strategies Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use ten frames. Ask a few students to explain their strategy for problem 2 aloud.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: work within 10 first (fact families for 3, 4, 7), and keep ten frames and counters out for every problem.
- Support: for missing-number problems, cover part of a group of counters with a cup and ask how many are hiding.
- Stretch: ask for two different strategies for 8 + 7 and which is faster; write equations with numbers on both sides (8 + 5 = ? + 6) and true-or-false problems for a partner.
- Multilingual learners: teach "same as", "missing", "true" and "false" with the balance and gestures (thumbs up, thumbs down). Keep the strategy names on an anchor chart with a picture for each.
- Watch for students who read = as "the answer is". When they say 7 = 8 - 1 is false "because the answer goes last", return to the balance.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are learning smart ways to add and subtract, such as making a ten (9 + 4 is the same as 10 + 3) and using doubles (if 6 + 6 = 12, then 6 + 7 = 13). Ask your child to show you their favorite strategy. Play "how many are hiding": put 12 spoons on the table, hide some under a towel, and ask how many are hiding if 5 are showing.",
  "id": "u4-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Adding and Subtracting Strategies",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{

The long hand shows the minutes.\nWe can count votes on a chart, too.\nIn this unit we will measure, tell time and read charts.",

files.codex/u5-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students order three objects by length and compare two lengths indirectly by using a third object (1.MD.A.1).
- Students measure length as a whole number of same-size units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps (1.MD.A.2).
- Students tell and write time in hours and half hours on analog and digital clocks (1.MD.B.3).
- Students organize, represent and interpret data with up to three categories, and answer how many in all and how many more (1.MD.C.4).

MATERIALS
- Connecting cubes, paper clips (all the same size) and string
- Classroom objects of different lengths to measure: pencils, books, shoes, ribbons
- A geared demonstration clock and a paper-plate clock for each student
- A class chart with three columns, sticky notes or tally marks
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read How Long? What Time? together. Line up three students by height, then compare two classroom objects that cannot be put side by side using a string. Lesson activity: How Long Is It?
Day 2: Measure and Compare. Measure objects with cubes in pairs. Show what happens when cubes have gaps or overlap (the number changes). Students complete the assignment.
Day 3: Clocks. Show the hour hand alone moving from 3 to 4. Then show 3:30, with the hour hand halfway. Students make times on paper-plate clocks and begin Clocks and Charts.
Day 4: Data. Take a class vote with three choices and record it as a chart. Ask: which got the most? how many more? how many in all? Students finish Clocks and Charts.
Day 5: Assessment: Measuring and Time Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use cubes and clocks.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give measuring strips with a start line. Measure only with cubes before paper clips. Use an hour-hand-only clock for hours before adding the minute hand.
- Support: for "how many more", line up the two groups of sticky notes and count the extras.
- Stretch: measure the same object with cubes and with paper clips and explain why the numbers differ; tell the time one hour later and one half hour later.
- Multilingual learners: teach longer, shorter, longest, shortest, hour, half past and o'clock with objects and the clock. Both "4:30" and "half past four" are correct; teach both.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are measuring, telling time and reading charts. At home, measure things with spoons or paper clips: how many spoons long is the table? Point out the clock at bedtime or dinnertime and ask your child what time it is, to the hour or half hour (7:00 or 7:30). You can also take a family vote, such as a favorite fruit, and count the votes together.",
  "id": "u5-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Measuring and Telling Time",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}

{
  "body": "What Makes a Shape?: 1. 3. 2. No; a shape's name comes from its sides and corners, not its color. 3. No; its sides are not all the same length (it is a rectangle). 4. Any closed shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners; yes, it is still a triangle.\nBuild New Shapes: the drawing shows two or more smaller shapes put together with their edges touching, and the student names the shapes used and the new shape (for example, two triangles make a square; two squares make a rectangle; four quarter-circles make a circle).\nHalves and Fourths: 1. A circle split by one line through the middle into 2 equal shares; each share is a half. 2. A rectangle split into 4 equal shares; each share is a fourth (or a quarter). 3. No; halves must be 2 equal shares, and these parts are not the same size. 4. One fourth (a quarter) of the pizza. 5. One half; when you cut the same pizza into more equal shares, each share is smaller.\nShapes and Shares Check: 1. 4 sides and 4 corners. 2. A triangle. 3. Any two shapes that make a rectangle, such as two squares, two smaller rectangles or two triangles. 4. A square split into 2 equal shares (one straight line across the middle, up and down, side to side or corner to corner). 5. A circle split into 4 equal shares with one share colored. 6. One half; fewer equal shares means bigger shares.\nScoring tip: shares only need to look about equal in a first grader's drawing; score the idea of equal shares, not ruler-straight lines. A student who says a fourth is bigger \"because 4 is more than 2\" is Not yet on problem 6; fold two paper circles to show it.",
  "id": "u6-answer-key",
  "purpose": "answer-key",

files.codex/u6-overview.json:
{
  "body": "Shapes are everywhere! 🔺 🟦 ⚪\nA triangle always has 3 sides and 3 corners, big or small, red or blue.\nWe can put shapes together to make new shapes.\nWe can cut shapes into equal parts called halves and fourths.\nIn this unit we will be shape detectives.",
  "id": "u6-overview",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Shape Detectives",
  "visibility": "students"
}
files.codex/u6-teacher-guide.json:
{
  "body": "OBJECTIVES
- Students tell defining attributes (closed, number of sides and corners) from non-defining attributes (color, size, which way it is turned), and draw shapes with given attributes (1.G.A.1).
- Students compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, triangles, half-circles and quarter-circles) to make a new shape (1.G.A.2).
- Students partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares as halves, fourths and quarters, and understand that more equal shares make smaller shares (1.G.A.3).

MATERIALS
- Pattern blocks and paper shapes in several sizes and colors (triangles, squares, rectangles, half-circles, quarter-circles)
- Geoboards and rubber bands, or dot paper
- Paper circles and rectangles for folding, and scissors
- A "shape detective" sorting mat: Is it a triangle? Yes / No
- Tablets with the class activities open, for photos of work

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Shape Detectives together. Lesson activity: What Makes a Shape? Sort a pile of paper shapes into triangles and not triangles, including skinny, turned and open ones. Ask: what clue did you use?
Day 2: Build New Shapes. Students make new shapes with pattern blocks (two triangles make a square, a square and two triangles make a trapezoid), trace them, and record themselves telling which shapes they used.
Day 3: Fold paper circles and rectangles in half. Are the two parts the same size? Then fold again to make fourths. Name them: halves, fourths, quarters. Students start Halves and Fourths.
Day 4: Finish Halves and Fourths. Share a pretend pizza: is a half or a fourth bigger? Cut two same-size paper circles to check. Return to unequal shares: why is the bigger piece not a half?
Day 5: Assessment: Shapes and Shares Check. Read each problem aloud. Students may use pattern blocks and paper shapes.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: give students shapes to hold and count sides and corners with a finger or sticker on each corner. Fold paper shapes before drawing lines.
- Support: for equal shares, start with rectangles, which are easier to fold evenly than circles.
- Stretch: find two different ways to cut a square into fourths (four small squares or four triangles); build one shape from as many smaller shapes as possible and count them.
- Multilingual learners: label each shape with its name and a picture. Teach side, corner, equal, half and fourth with hands-on folding. Note that "quarter" and "fourth" mean the same here.
- Watch for students who call a turned square a "diamond": it is still a square because its sides and corners did not change.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are shape detectives! We are learning that a shape's name comes from its sides and corners, not its color or size, and we are cutting shapes into halves and fourths. At snack time, ask your child to cut a sandwich or a tortilla into two equal shares, then four. Ask: which piece is bigger, a half or a fourth? Go on a shape hunt around the house too.",
  "id": "u6-teacher-guide",
  "purpose": "context",
  "title": "Teacher guide: Shapes and Equal Shares",
  "visibility": "teacher-only"
}
